newsitem.title: USA: Probers seek evidence of "serial bomber" in Atlanta.
newsitem.headline: Probers seek evidence of "serial bomber" in Atlanta.

text.p: Investigators continued their search for possible links between a bomb that exploded at a gay and lesbian nightclub in Atlanta on Friday and two other unsolved bombings which have shaken the city over the past seven months.

A police cordon sealed off streets for several blocks around The Otherside Lounge on Saturday as agents from the FBI, the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms (ATF), the Georgia state police and local law enforcement agencies combed through the neighbourhood for pieces of shrapnel and other evidence.

Members of special FBI and ATF response teams arrived from other parts of the country to assist in the investigation, and authorities predicted the number of federal agents working on the case would reach the 100 mark before Monday.
Investigators said the attack bore similarities to two other incidents in Atlanta -- a January double-bombing at an abortion clinic and the deadly Centennial Olympic Park bombing last July.
That fact led a senior FBI official in Atlanta to speculate that investigators could be dealing with a serial bomber.

"The bombings have not been categorically tied together yet. Of course, the last bombing was aimed at an abortion clinic. It's a possibility that this one was motivated by hate," said FBI spokesman Jay Spadafore.

The nightclub bomb, apparently packed with nails, went off in the rear patio section of the lounge in northeast Atlanta shortly before 10 p.m. EST (0300 GMT Friday). Staff said the club, frequented mostly by lesbians, was about half full at the time.
Police found a second bomb in a backpack hidden among some bushes in an adjacent parking lot and detonated the device with a remote-control robot.
Both police and nightclub staff said there were no prior warnings and no claims of responsibility for the attack.

"We all recognise that there are similarities here. We will be searching out the possibility that we have a serial bomber," Woody Johnson, the special agent in charge of the Atlanta FBI office, told a news conference.

Of the five people hurt in the blast, only one was seriously injured. She was identified as Memrie Wells-Crestwell of Snellville, Ga. A spokesman for Grady Memorial Hospital said she underwent surgery to remove shrapnel from her right shoulder and was later listed in stable condition.
Homosexual rights activists condemned the bombing as a hate crime reminiscent of Ku Klux Klan attacks on black civil rights activists in the South in the 1960s.
The National Gay and Lesbian Task Force wrote to President Bill Clinton, pressing him to "speak out loudly" against the attack.

Under federal law, the Justice Department can investigate a crime as bias-motivated if it might have been driven by hate against a certain race, religion, national origin or disability. The statutes do not include sexual orientation.
Wells-Crestwell, who was initially believed to have been shot, rolled up her sleeve to find a three- to four-inch (8-10 cm) nail sticking through her arm, according to eyewitnesses.
Federal officials sought leads from the public through the special ATF hotline, 1-888-ATF-BOMB.

Police investigators said Friday's bombing was similar to a double-bomb attack on an Atlanta abortion clinic in January that injured half a dozen people, mostly law enforcement agents and rescue workers.
As in that attack, the second device at the nightclub was placed in an apparent attempt to injure police and rescue workers responding to the initial emergency call.

The use of a backpack for the second device resembled the Centennial Olympic Park bombing in July. In that incident, a pipe bomb packed with nails and hidden in a green military-style knapsack exploded during a crowded outdoor concert in downtown Atlanta, leaving two people dead and more than 100 wounded.
